M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., and Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, vol. 7, pp. 453–466. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a_00276
creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov (Google Research)
description: Natural Questions (NQ) is a question answering dataset where questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Annotators are presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results and annotate a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or mark null if no answer is present. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations, 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development, and 7,842 examples with 5-way annotations sequestered as test data.
name: Natural Questions
rai:annotationsPerItem: Training examples have single annotations (1-way); development and test examples have 5-way annotations; a subset of 302 examples has 25-way annotations for analysis of human variability.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post-hoc evaluation of annotation quality was performed by four expert annotators (the paper's first four authors) who independently classified a sample of 139 non-null examples into Correct (C), Correct but debatable (Cd), and Wrong (W) categories, then reached consensus. Long answer precision (ˆΨ) was 90% and short answer precision was 84%. Additionally, 25-way annotations on 302 examples were analyzed to study variability: the most popular long answer accounts for 83% of annotations; the two most popular account for 96%. For short answers, the most popular accounts for 64% and the top three for 90%. A super-annotator upper bound was established: 90.0% precision, 84.6% recall, 87.2% F1 for long answers; 79.1% precision, 72.6% recall, 75.7% F1 for short answers.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators are presented with a (question, Wikipedia page) pair and complete three conceptual stages: (1) Question Identification — determine if the question is "good" (fact-seeking, answerable with an entity or explanation) or "bad" (ambiguous, incomprehensible, opinion-seeking, etc.); (2) Long Answer Identification — for good questions, select the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, or whole list) containing enough information to infer the answer, or mark "no answer"; (3) Short Answer Identification — for examples with long answers, select the entity or set of entities within the long answer, flag yes/no, or flag that no short answer is possible. Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was constantly monitored. Average annotation time was 80 seconds per example.
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges that focusing on Wikipedia as the evidence source may introduce biases, as Wikipedia is a specific source of factual information with its own stylistic and coverage biases. The dataset focuses on longer queries (8+ words) as more complex questions, which excludes shorter queries. "How to" questions are excluded. The paper notes that future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, "how to" questions, or domains other than Wikipedia.
rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries of 8 words or more issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time. Simple heuristics filter questions from the query stream (e.g., starting with "who", "when", "where", or containing multiple entities). Questions are then run through the Google search engine and kept only where there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results. The resulting (question, Wikipedia page) pairs are presented to human annotators who identify long answers (HTML bounding boxes such as paragraphs, tables, or lists) and short answers (entity spans or yes/no) on the Wikipedia page.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine (queries of 8 words or more issued by multiple users in a short period of time), paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results for each query.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses only on longer queries (8+ words), excluding shorter queries and "how to" questions. Evidence is limited to Wikipedia pages, which may introduce domain and coverage biases. Boolean (yes/no) answers are not addressed in the baseline experiments and are left to future work. The annotation task involves genuine ambiguity about whether a paragraph contains all evidence required to answer a question, leading to annotator variability. The test set is sequestered.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered from the Google search query stream using heuristics to retain fact-seeking questions of 8 words or more (e.g., starting with "who", "when", "where" with specific grammatical patterns, or containing multiple entities with adjectives/adverbs/verbs). Part-of-speech tags and entities were identified using Google's Cloud NLP API. Hearst patterns were used to pre-define categorical noun phrases. Only queries where a Wikipedia page appeared in the top 5 search results were retained.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that a solution to Natural Questions will have genuine utility to users seeking information, and that it is better equipped as a benchmark for NLU than trivia-based tasks. Progress on this benchmark is expected to drive significant advances in natural language understanding, with direct utility in real-world question answering applications.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as: (1) a large-scale end-to-end training dataset for the question answering problem; (2) a benchmark dataset to drive research in natural language understanding (NLU); (3) a resource to study human performance in providing QA annotations for naturally occurring questions. It is designed to evaluate open-domain question answering systems that must identify both long answers (evidence passages) and short answers (entity spans) from Wikipedia pages.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API (https://cloud.google.com/natural-language) was used to identify part-of-speech tags and named entities during question filtering. Hearst patterns were used to pre-define categorical noun phrases for the heuristic filters.

null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: The paper only states there was a pool of around 50 annotators with an average annotation time of 80 seconds; no demographic information (nationality, language background, expertise level beyond being annotators) is provided.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data handling; queries without a Wikipedia page in top 5 results are simply discarded (not treated as missing data to be imputed).
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe or date range for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; missing/null answers are explicitly labeled as NULL rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation, augmentation, or resampling of the dataset itself is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper explicitly states questions are anonymized aggregated queries; no personal or sensitive information is collected or discussed.
